cards.source_text: An Open Letter from Academics about AI Risk / Life Without the Internet & the Case for Non-Network Redundancy There has been an increase in concern over AI destroying humanity, most recently spurred by tweets from former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon about how dangerous AI is, and a follow-up tweet from current employee Evan Hubinger, who said “Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe A.I. could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.” Some in the AI world are calling for “the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development” and there has been much discussion of trying to slow down or stop all AI research. Now, a new open letter is circulating, this time from academics worried about the possibility of a “global catastrophe” resulting from AI, calling for political leaders to “create an international treaty, much like the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.” It was written by philosopher Molly Gardner (University of Florida) and made public yesterday. If you’re interested in reading or signing it, it’s here: “Open Letter from Academics Concerning Recent Developments in Artificial Intelligence“. What follows are some thoughts of mine about one approach to mitigating AI risk. I don’t intend to discourage people from signing the “Open Letter from Academics Concerning Recent Developments in Artificial Intelligence“—it couldn’t hurt to do so. But for various reasons, I think efforts to slow or pause or stop AI research face an insurmountable collective action problem. Even if the well-known corporations working on AI cease their efforts (itself highly unlikely), research and development will continue. AI tools are relevantly not like nuclear weapons, insofar as work to create and improve them is much less detectable, so enforcement will be extremely difficult or invasive. And since the claims about AI destroying humanity are speculative, the scenarios they describe are unprecedented, and AI is not seen unambiguously as a weapon, there will be insufficient will to implement a regime of punishment (on individuals, corporations, nations) severe enough to effectively enforce cooperation. I don’t know more about AI than people like Coxon and Hubinger, and while I’m not fully convinced of their pessimism, I haven’t read anything (yet) by other knowledgeable people to show me they’re wrong. cards.source_text: The idea that autonomous, thinking machines may one day destroy property, hierarchy and inequality is as old as western political thought. In Aristotle’s Politics, the philosopher cites a fantasy from the Iliad, in which machines begin to act independently of human direction, concluding: “If every tool could perform its own work when ordered, or by seeing what to do in advance … if thus shuttles wove and quills played harps of themselves, master-craftsmen would have no need of assistants and masters no need of slaves.” The dream that automation could inaugurate a classless society is also present in the writings of Karl Marx. In 1858 he imagined the replacement of intellectual property with “socialised knowledge”, which would merge into a “general intellect”, blowing the foundations of capitalism sky high. Today this prospect has begun to haunt Silicon Valley. In July, Dean Ball, head of strategic futures at OpenAI, claimed China’s advocacy of open-source models of artificial intelligence might bring about “full AI communism”. For China, Ball complained, “AI is a public good which will ultimately be provided by the state as a kind of ‘digital public infrastructure’.” This, he concluded, “strikes me as a dystopian hellscape”. Though I relish Ball’s discomfort, I doubt the rise of rival Chinese models – Kimi, Qwen and Deepseek – heralds the end of capitalism. Rather, it is an attempt to counter one strategy for global domination with another. The US AI strategy – which is to hoard computing power, giving users access only via the internet – is designed to force the rest of us to use American software, cloud computing services and regulations. The Chinese counterplay is to make the AI open source, allowing users to run versions locally on their own servers and to firewall their data from being exploited by a Chinese AI provider. Beijing gambles that if AI does indeed become a “general purpose technology”, the People’s Republic of China can win the battle for supremacy in the technologies built on top of it, such as brain-machine interfaces, bioengineering and what it calls the “low altitude economy” (the realm of delivery drones, and so on). cards.source_text: How Different Are Philosophers? (guest post) “Do philosophers really think differently than non-philosophers?” That’s the question taken up by a team of researchers in a recent study published in Philosophical Psychology. Focusing on differences between philosophers and non-philosophers in regard to neurodivergent traits and responses to thought experiments, the researchers found some support, in the aggregate, for a “yes” answer to that question. The following guest post is by Thomas Nadelhoffer (College of Charleston), and is based on the article, “Thinking Differently: Neurodivergent Traits and Responses to Thought Experiments in Philosophers and the General Population,” co-authored with Paul McKee (Duke), Khaoula Boulhadi (Southern Connecticut State), and Helena Weymouth (College of Charleston). How Different Are Philosophers? by Thomas Nadelhoffer “The history of philosophy is to a great extent that of a certain clash of human temperaments [. . .] Yet, his temperament really gives him a stronger bias than any of his more strictly objective premises. It loads the evidence for him one way or the other” — William James Neurodiversity and Philosophical Intuitions In addition to being abstract thinkers, philosophers are stereotyped as being argumentative, overly self-absorbed in their own thoughts, and enjoy creating increasingly fine distinctions regarding everyday terms while imagining novel hypothetical situations and debating the conclusions they draw. It’s possible that many philosophers have quite distinctive personalities. More than two millennia before the modern notion of stereotypes existed, Plato used humor to poke fun at philosophers in the Theaetetus by telling a story of Thales contemplating the stars, so engrossed that he forgot where he was walking and fell down a well. However, do philosophers really think differently than non-philosophers? This was one of the questions behind the paper we recently published in Philosophical Psychology. We surveyed 1,254 individuals, 632 with formal training in philosophy and 622 members of the general public, and explored whether philosophers exhibit significant cognitive differences from non-philosophers using multiple measures of neurodiverse traits. To get enough responses from philosophers, we recruited participants here at Daily Nous and on Leiter Reports. We recruited the general population participants from Prolific. We preregistered our experimental design, research questions, and hypotheses. Phil

cards.source_text: It’s an ungainly word for English speakers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gleichschaltung. Yet the concept remains central for a clear view of what happened to Germany in the 1930s. In 1933, the nation completely transformed, seemingly overnight, through “a concerted policy of ‘coordination’ (Gleichschaltung),” the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum writes. “Culture, the economy, education, and law all came under Nazi control.” Those artists and organizations that were not purged had their essential character changed to reflect an entirely different set of artistic and political values. One publication, especially, serves as an example of the Nazification of culture. The arts journal Jugend (Youth), writes Messy Nessy Chic, “had been turned largely into propaganda” between 1933 and 1940, its final year. But prior to the regime’s takeover, Jugend showcased the most avant-garde, “degenerate” artists of the era, and might have been “the ‘brainiest’ periodical of the day,” as one critic wrote in a 1904 issue of The Yale Literary Magazine. “There is no magazine published in England or in this country which is at all like it.” You can take a look yourself—browse, search, and download hundreds of scanned issues of Jugend at the University of Heidelberg’s digital archive, thousands of pages in PDF form, spanning the magazine’s forty-four-year history. You can also see images at Flickr. As in England, France, Austria, and the U.S., the Art Nouveau movement in Germany emerged from a whirlwind of post-Impressionist painting, Orientalist motifs, folk art, modernist art and advertising, book illustration, and graphic and industrial design. Appropriately, given its perch on the threshold of a new century, Art Nouveau looked both backward—to the medieval, gothic, and Romantic—and forward toward a more modernist, urbane, and urbanized sensibility. cards.source_text: Frank Lloyd Wright was often strapped for cash. In that respect, he had something in common with Vincent van Gogh, who passed most of his much shorter life in more dire circumstances. Unlike Wright, who enjoyed decades of fame at the pinnacle of the American architectural profession, van Gogh remained practically unknown until after his death. But if they’ve encountered one another in the afterlife, they’ve certainly discussed one subject above all others: their shared appreciation for Japanese woodblock prints. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured the collection of 500 such works of art that van Gogh left behind. At the end of Wright’s life in 1959, he owned about 6,000, many of which his estate had to sell to pay both Japanese art dealers and American tax collectors. We could say that Wright died as he lived, advanced age having not evidently diminished either his financial recklessness or his obsession with ukiyo‑e. The masters of that classical “art of the floating world” like Hokusai and Hiroshige were among his favorite artists of any kind. When still a teenager, Wright went to work for the architect Joseph Silsbee, who’d built a chapel for his uncle. “Silsbee’s cousin, Ernest Fenollosa, happened to be the world’s leading Western expert on Japanese art at the time,” writes Kevin Nute at The Conversation. It isn’t certain how well the young Wright knew Fenollosa — or indeed when he began collecting ukiyo‑e, writes Frank Lloyd Wright and the Art of Japan author Julia Meech-Pekarik, though he may have seen both Hokusai and Hiroshige’s works at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, “about the time he opened his practice in Oak Park.” Eight years later, “Wright made his first voyage to Japan in pursuit of prints, and he did indeed return with enough expertise to stage an exhibition of his own Hiroshige collection at the Art Institute of Chicago in March of 1906.” He returned for two months in 1913, making it clear that he was only interested in using that time to acquire more prints. Later, while working on the Imperial Hotel between 1917 and 1922, he spent a total of more than three years there, later writing that “the pursuit of the Japanese print became my constant recreation while in Tokio,” a quest whose “adventures and excursions would take place at night or sometimes call for a journey by day to distant places.” This positioned him well to take on a sideline as a dealer (or as he liked to call himself, a merchant) of Japan

cards.source_text: When Emily St John Mandel was a child she had a dream that would stay with her for decades. It was a nightmare in which “I was trying to find my dad in a crowd, and there were other people who looked like him but weren’t him”, she says. “It just kind of struck my imagination.” Forty-ish years later, Mandel’s seventh novel, Exit Party, opens with a gathering in Los Angeles, 2031, where bizarre things happen. Doubles of some guests appear. Someone else disappears altogether. The novel then alternates between two potential future Americas, one riven by the chaos of civil war, the other a surveillance state. Doppelgangers and alternative realities are having a cultural moment in our uncanny, deepfake times. Mandel says the biggest challenge western democracy faces is “the collapse of consensual reality. When you get to a situation where half the electorate disagrees on basic reality – for example, who won an election, or is Covid real? I don’t know how you come back from that.” On a more personal level, she has always been fascinated by what she calls “the counter-life – the one where you took a different job or married a different person. The way that, if we made a different decision, we would have become a somewhat different person.” This interest comes, she thinks, from a feeling that “my life as a writer in New York City is a bit improbable”. Mandel was home-schooled on a tiny island in British Columbia, Canada, before training as a dancer. As she puts it, she was “essentially not educated until I was about 15 … I haven’t got a high school diploma.” She wrote while working office jobs until her third novel, Station Eleven, became a smash hit. The 2014 story of life after a global pandemic felt so prescient when readers rediscovered it during Covid that she developed a reputation for clairvoyance. It has sold 1.5m copies and been translated into 37 languages. Her novels since – The Glass Hotel and Sea of Tranquility – were global bestsellers too. It’s a staggering career, and, as she sees it: “There are a million ways this might not have happened.” We meet on a sunny New York City day, in the lobby of a sleek Williamsburg hotel. She’s off to have a haircut after we meet, even though her neat pixie cut scarcely looks trimmable. cards.source_text: In some rare cases, adaptations and interpretations of a literary work can surpass the source. Despite hundreds of valiant efforts on the part of fans, filmmakers, game/toy designers, and radio producers, this has never been true of the fully-realized fantasy world in J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings trilogy (not that it’s ever been anyone’s intent). As we noted in a previous post, Tolkien’s fictional world is so intricate, its sources so vast and varied, that Corey Olsen, “The Tolkien Professor,” has made it his entire life’s work to open that world up to students and curious readers, such as with his eight-part lecture series on The Hobbit. One might also add illustrators to the list of Tolkien interpreters above who have—in the almost ninety years since The Hobbit’s publication and more than seventy years since the first appearance of The Lord of the Rings trilogy—done their best to visualize Tolkien’s world. But perhaps no one did so better than the master himself. Long known as a visual artist as well as a literary one, Tolkien left behind over 100 illustrations for The Hobbit, one of which adorns 2011’s HarperCollins 75th anniversary edition of the book. He also created these original cover designs for each book in The Lord of the Rings trilogy. In the long and complex publication history of Tolkien’s most famous of works, it’s unclear if these designs ever made it onto books published during his lifetime, but the sigil in the center of The Fellowship of the Ring design (above), with its ominous eye of Sauron surrounded by elvish runes and topped by the one ring, did grace the elegant, minimalist covers of the first edition of the trilogy. Tolkien’s artwork received a thorough treatment in a 1995 monograph J.R.R. Tolkien Artist & Illustrator, which covers over 60 years of Tolkien’s life as an artist, and the magic of flickr brings us this compendium of Tolkien illustrations. There, he was immediately surrounded by a crowd of people, who begged him to help one of their neighbours. And so, dismounting from his horse, he went to the man’s house, where he was confronted by the disturbing sight of a possessed man ‘lying prostrate with his head tied to a post and each of his hands to great stakes fixed in the ground.’ Despite these restraints, the man constantly writhed around, rolling his eyes, gnashing his teeth, and sticking his tongue out. To Hugh, as to the local onlookers, the diagnosis was clear: this unfortunate sailor had been possessed by a demon and could be cured only by an exorcism. Once the necessary rituals were performed, he was ‘delivered from the demon [and] … after living devoutly for some years, finally made a good and peaceful end.’ For Hugh’s biographer, Adam of Eynsham, the incident was worth recounting because it demonstrated not only that the future saint had healing powers, but that he was a brave and compassionate man (in sharp contrast to the local bishop, who had ‘galloped away as if pursued by the Furies’, rather than face a possessed man). But, to us, the story – full of fear, cruelty and superstition – sums up both everything that was wrong with medieval attitudes to mental illness, and the apparent uselessness of medieval medicine in the face of serious illness. And yet, as is so often the case when studying the distant past, the reality was rather more complicated. Influenced by stories of demonic possession (and there are lots of them, especially in saints’ lives and miracle collections), I long assumed that our ancestors’ attitudes to, and experiences of, mental health were completely different to our own – and that they would have little sympathy with our fast-growing mental health crisis. cards.source_text: In the beginning, Art of Noise were as much a provocation as a pop group. You could tell something was up just by looking at the list of personnel: a computer programmer, a composer and arranger, a recording engineer, a producer, and a journalist. The band—some of them, anyway—played instruments that looked like space-station command centers, collecting bits of audio from everyday life and arranging them into block-rocking beats, with fragmentary voices criss-crossing in digitally orchestrated counterpoint and car engines standing in for tambourines. The music was sly and funny in a postmodern way that had only recently been enabled by the emergence of digital sampling technology. It delighted in its own fakeness; drew melodies out of non-musical detritus and used traditional instruments as punchlines; approached recorded sound itself as both pigment and canvas. There was no singing, per se, unless it had been chopped up and rearranged at the command center. They hardly performed in public and wore eerie kabuki-like masks in photographs. Somehow, they had a Top 10 hit. Paul Morley’s role in this startling enterprise was primarily a conceptual one: lore-enforcement agent, to use a title some troupe of cheeky youngsters really should nick for themselves, bestowed on him in a 1985 ZigZag magazine profile of ZTT Records, the swashbuckling avant-pop label for which Art of Noise served for a time as a sort of faceless avatar and house band. According to one Art of Noise member, interviewed about In Visible Silence, their strange, brilliant, and oft-overlooked second album, Morley’s only concrete contributions to the earlier releases were the names of the songs. It was just a few months after the ZigZag piece, but a schism within Art of Noise had transpired, one that the British press covered with a fervor it generally reserved for bands with lead singers. The lore-enforcement types were on one side and the people who made the records were on the other. No score yet, be the first to add. Morley was a former NME scribbler whose high-flying prose and messianic certitude could make a manifesto of a grocery list, to say nothing of an album review. cards.source_text: “I never actually wanted to be a DJ,” Simon Green, better known as versatile electronic producer Bonobo, recently told Mixmag. “It just kind of happened by accident.” Now, after 26 years spent exploring the nuances of downtempo and house music, he wants off the album-tour hamster wheel. Distance in Static is likely his last Bonobo album, he says—at least “in a traditional sense.” The British musician recently moved from Southern California to Japan and is eyeing film scores, art installations, and modular string quartets with Miguel Atwood-Ferguson as potential next steps. But for all his ostensible desire to stretch, he retreads familiar ground on Distance in Static. Bonobo’s eighth album is his clubbiest album yet, a reflection of the sounds and textures that have shaped his evolution from downtempo mood-setter to headlining dance act. More victory lap than self-contained artist statement, it completes a trio of records—following his last two full-lengths, Migration and Fragments—that get progressively heavier in sound but lighter in ideas. No score yet, be the first to add. Migration had, among many things, good timing on its side; released in 2017, it coincided with the post-EDM rush to reimagine what contemporary dance floors could sound like, and Green’s sensual, club-lite soundscapes perfectly met the moment—funky synths and devotional vocals drizzled over variations of UK bass music, often backed by live bands and full string sections. But that chill-adjacent formula doesn’t sparkle like it used to, and Distance in Static feels recycled, lacking the freshness and exploratory spirit that made Green’s earlier work interesting. While Black Sands-era Bonobo was intriguingly hard to categorize—glitchy, funky, jazzy, and dubby, too heavy for “chill” and too heady for “club”—Distance in Static sounds as if each track was engineered to suit specific environments or playlists. There are groovy R&B-soul excursions like the Joy Crookes team-up “Always on Your Side,” sleek cosmic interludes like “ID700” and “Uncasually,” and billowing, eyes-closed, stadium-rave cuts like “Drift” and “Cycles,” which echo each other’s mournful, heartstring-tugging synths. Despite Green’s determination to play in multiple sandboxes, the tidily siloed nature of these tracks also makes them feel more anonymous. “Me and You,” the project’s catchy lead single, should be a slam dunk—it’s bouncy, playful, tightly edited, and samples a 1950 Malawian field recording by ethnomusicologist

Willis, who cut her teeth wielding the state’s racketeering laws to prosecute schoolteachers, claimed (often through the use of lyrics, social media captions, and tattoos) that YSL was a front for “Young Slime Life,” a gang associated with the Bloods. She alleged a violent conspiracy that indicted 28 co-defendants, including YSL artists Gunna, Yak Gotti, and Duke, along with label head Young Thug, but failed to win convictions on the most serious charges. Still, Willis claims an “amazing” job done—an understandable position if you consider the stipulations of Thug’s freedom: 15 years of probation, a 10-year ban from Atlanta city limits, and a tarnished brand. The video for “Money on Money,” Young Thug’s first single post-RICO trial, opened with an image of the former YSL logo going up in flames. No longer on good terms (or legally allowed to communicate) with many of YSL’s foundational artists, and presumably still mourning the loss of his protégé, Lil Keed (who tragically passed from health complications in 2022, shortly into Thug’s 30-month prison stint), it would’ve been understandable if Thug had retreated from the spotlight, guard up. cards.source_text: In his 20s, when Nate Amos was uploading his every musical impulse to Bandcamp, he released a particularly out-there tranche of songs focused on “technology corrupting nature,” he told the Guardian recently. He soon came to understand this noisy spell as a symptom of anxiety and depression: “The beauty was in the unknown, because I was having such a hard time with the known.” The newer work that’s made his name as This Is Lorelei is tellingly lucid by contrast, the work of someone who can now look discomfort dead on and make it beautiful. It doesn’t take a leap to connect that to Amos’ recent sobriety. His official debut album, 2024’s Box for Buddy, Box for Star—a crystalline pop record that stealthily acquired masterpiece status, affirmed by an all-star reimagining—came after he addressed his alcohol and substance use. Where some people claim to undergo a total personality overhaul alongside such a shift, Amos considered that idea and found it dishonest. You can hear it in Box’s many irrepressible styles, and in how he let his timeless pop songs loosen into more diffuse arrangements to reject the idea of too-tidy resolution: a sign that he wasn’t just an economical writer with an eye for tightly nested imagery (“And I know it’s only cards/But love I feel your heart in spades”) but an equally intentional composer. No score yet, be the first to add. The Singer in My Band pushes further into almost prelapsarian simplicity: skippy, scuffed country-leaning songs perky with twang and walking basslines. Amos whittles endlessly charming melodies like one of those roadside carpenters equally capable of carving a duck as a motorbike. Hat-tipping to his bluegrass whiz dad (who adds an electrifying banjo to the title track), the tighter sound means Singer doesn’t have the magpie dazzle of Box. But even within those limitations, Amos continues to prove he’s one of those people who’s just good at everything: would-be standards, picaresque capers; cowpunk farce, burning frustration, purest heartbreak. “You were right to go, don’t you think so?/When I wouldn’t trade a good night for a better day,” he sings on “And I Haven’t Seen My Love in Quite a While,” a self-lacerating take on the record’s theme of whether you can outrun your true nature. The close focus of the sound underscores the feeling that Amos is puzzling all this out in earnest. The music that seeps through the speakers is lite funk rock, undoubtedly influenced by the Japanese pop artists DeMarco has long cribbed from. “Just garbage,” he chuckles, but nearly 5 million people seem to disagree, to the point of concern for his standards or even his mental health. cards.source_text: More than 500 people have invaded Brazil’s Ituna/Itatá Indigenous Land in recent weeks, opening illegal roads, setting deliberate fires and threatening federal agents. The area is home to the Igarapé Ipiaçava Indigenous people who live in voluntary isolation with no contact with outsiders. On Aug. 26, a federal court ordered the government to deploy the National Public Security Force within 48 hours to contain the invasion. As of Sept 11, the forces hadn’t yet arrived. The recent invasion followed the creation of the Bacajaí Environmental Protection Area (APA Bacajaí) under a new state law, which allows private landowners to build homes and raise livestock. However, APA Bacajaí completely overlaps the federally protected Indigenous land in Pará state, creating legal confusion that authorities say has been weaponized by land-grabbers to justify occupation for cattle ranching and other agricultural activities. The Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office (MPF) has asked a federal court to fine the government 50,000 Brazilian reais (about $9,000) daily for failing to deploy enough security forces to contain the invasion. The area is currently under a temporary land-use restriction order to protect the isolated people living there. The government has argued it needs authorization from Pará’s government, which hasn’t cooperated. However, federal prosecutors say the federal government can be deployed on federal land without state authorization. Both the federal government and the state of Pará did not reply to Mongabay’s requests for comment by the time of publication. In its press statement, the MPF said the Indigenous Affairs Agency (Funai) and Federal Police overflights have detected the use of heavy machinery and chainsaws to clear more than 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) of forest trails and clandestine roads to mark illegal plots in the Indigenous land. The author, who was 51 years old and had published only one book before, said she hoped her new one, out that year, would become a classic. “But then straight away I said: ‘Only joking!’ Because I didn’t want to sound full of myself, and I certainly didn’t think the wish would come true,” she remembers today. That author is Julia Donaldson; the book she published in 1999 was The Gruffalo; and, as you hardly need telling, her wish did indeed come true. And how. Since its publication, more than 18.2m copies of The Gruffalo and its sequel have sold worldwide. The Gruffalo’s Child was published in 2004, and together these tales of the terrible creature with terrible claws, and terrible teeth in his terrible jaws, have helped Donaldson to sell more than 50m books in the UK. In 2025 she was named the country’s bestselling author – across all genres, children’s and adult’s – since records began. Now the Gruffalo is making what Donaldson – who was made a dame in June – confirms will be his final outing. Gruffalo Granny, out this week, extends the protagonist’s family back a generation. In the new book, the Gruffalo and his daughter are awaiting a visit from Granny Gruffalo. The mouse, who played a pivotal role in the first and second books, is again centre stage; and longtime characters owl, fox and snake are all part of the action too. When we meet in a swish hotel in central London, I’m struck by the similarities between Donaldson and her new character. Her hair, like the Gruffalo Granny’s fur, is grey; in Donaldson’s case, it’s a neat bob, curled under at the ends. She is wearing a blue floral dress and navy shoes, and when she smiles her eyes twinkle; but I suspect that, like the Gruffalo Granny, she has prickles that reveal themselves when needed. cards.source_text: I have to confess that I rarely enjoy birding in montane cloud forests. The birds that live in these mountainous, cool and humid habitats are masters of disguise, usually passing themselves off as a leaf or other form of foliage. But if I want to see antpittas – elusive, ground-dwelling birds that rarely show themselves – then I have no choice. So, on a cool, cloudy morning my guide, Juan Carlos Crespo, Fredy Ramón Castillo, a local ranger, and I are standing on a steep, muddy path close to Tapichalaca Lodge, 2,500 metres above sea level in the eastern Andes, waiting for the jocotoco antpitta to emerge from the undergrowth. Fortunately, antpittas have a soft spot for food, especially the large, juicy earthworms Castillo has placed on a low branch nearby. He calls the bird, with increasingly loud and urgent shouts of “venga, venga!” (“come on, come on!”). The minutes tick by, until I begin to wonder if this is a lost cause. Then, out of nowhere, a plump, thrush-sized bird with a chestnut back, grey front, black crown and white face-patch materialises just a few feet away. It proceeds to gulp down the earthworms as if it has not eaten for days. I have seen a lot of different birds, but never one that so changed the course of bird conservation. In November 1997, a group led by the influential US ornithologist Robert Ridgely was exploring this area of southern Ecuador to see what they could find. As they ascended a forest trail at dawn, they heard the sound of a bird in the far distance. As Ridgely recalled many years later, “It had this crazy call, sounding like an owl; but we had no idea what it was, and to be honest I never thought we would find out.” Ridgely walked ahead of the group, and heard the sound much closer than before. He recorded the call and played it back to the mystery creature, which came crashing through the dense bamboo, right out into the open. “I knew right away that this was something really special, which no one apart from the local people had ever seen – an entirely new species to science.” It was, in fact, one of the greatest ornithological breakthroughs of the late 20th century: while new species are sometimes discovered, they are rarely so large, noisy and so obviously different from other members of their family. Talking to local farmers, Ridgely discovered that they were familiar with the bird, which they had named “jocotoco” to represent its loud, barking call. cards.source_text: - Scientists have formally described Mus dumbara, a new species of spiny mouse from Sri Lanka’s Dumbara or Knuckles Mountain Range after years of waiting. - Collected for the first time in 2004, it took more than two decades of morphological and genetic analysis to establish it as a distinct species from the other spiny mouse species found in Sri Lanka. - Subsequent efforts to find fresh specimens of the elusive mouse proved unsuccessful, despite around 1,900 trap nights in the area, leaving scientists with limited information about its current population and distribution. - Found only from a small area of the Knuckles Range so far, the discovery highlights the island’s overlooked biodiversity of small mammals and the need for further surveys to understand the species’ ecology and conservation needs. COLOMBO — As dusk settled over the paddy fields at Puwakpitiya, a village on the northern edge of Knuckles Mountain Range locally known as Dumbara mountains in Central Sri Lanka, researchers began laying traps along the uneasy boundary between farmland and forest. They were targeting small terrestrial mammals moving through the landscape. On the ground, drift fences were created to lead animals to pitfall traps, while box style Sherman live traps were baited with feed. But the usual rodent lure — peanut butter — failed to attract the mice in Sri Lanka, so the researchers instead turned to something more familiar to the local mice — pieces of burnt coconut. On March 11, 2004, one of the pitfall traps caught a small mouse that looked different. Six days later, a second specimen was caught in a baited trap. Both were females, not larger than a child’s palm, with fulvous-gray pelage broken by spiny guard hairs and a slender, naked tail longer than the head and body. Externally, the animal resembled Mayor’s mouse (Mus mayori), a species endemic to Sri Lanka’s highlands, but differed in tail length and head shape, offering initial clues about a new species. The two mice remained a scientific mystery for more than two decades, but careful genetic and morphological evidence finally confirmed what researchers had suspected all along, and they soon introduced a species new to science. It’s been named Mus dumbara, commonly known as the Dumbara valley’s spiny mouse, a name that links the rodent to its locality. items.summary: “Do philosophers really think differently than non-philosophers?” That’s the question taken up by a team of researchers in a recent study published in Philosophical Psychology. Focusing on differences between philosophers and non-philosophers in regard to neurodivergent traits and responses to thought experiments, the researchers found some support, in the aggregate, for a “yes” answer to that question. The following guest post is by Thomas Nadelhoffer (College of Charleston), and is based on the article, “Thinking Differently: Neurodivergent Traits and Responses to Thought Experiments in Philosophers and the General Population,” co-authored with Paul McKee (Duke), Khaoula Boulhadi (Southern Connecticut State), and Helena Weymouth (College of Charleston). How Different Are Philosophers? by Thomas Nadelhoffer “The history of philosophy is to a great extent that of a certain clash of human temperaments [. . .] Yet, his temperament really gives him a stronger bias than any of his more strictly objective premises. items.title: AI will transform capitalism – but how?
items.summary: Technology is going to drastically reshape the economy, and it’s within our power to decide what that looks like The idea that autonomous, thinking machines may one day destroy property, hierarchy and inequality is as old as western political thought. In Aristotle’s Politics, the philosopher cites a fantasy from the Iliad, in which machines begin to act independently of human direction, concluding: “If every tool could perform its own work when ordered, or by seeing what to do in advance … if thus shuttles wove and quills played harps of themselves, master-craftsmen would have no need of assistants and masters no need of slaves.” The dream that automation could inaugurate a classless society is also present in the writings of Karl Marx. In 1858 he imagined the replacement of intellectual property with “socialised knowledge”, which would merge into a “general intellect”, blowing the foundations of capitalism sky high. That author is Julia Donaldson; the book she published in 1999 was The Gruffalo; and, as you hardly need telling, her wish did indeed come true. And how.
